digestIntro: Today's throughline is AI narrative control. The industry — with Washington's backing — is actively rebranding itself as "superintelligence" to outrun public backlash, and that messaging fight is exactly the terrain your practice sits on: how institutions and brands talk about AI is now a strategic choice, not a technical one. Watch how this collides with the Capilano data-centre protest at your doorstep, where community resistance to AI infrastructure is already live on a BC campus.
whyItMatters: Today's throughline is AI narrative control. The industry — with Washington's backing — is actively rebranding itself as "superintelligence" to outrun public backlash, and that messaging fight is exactly the terrain your practice sits on: how institutions and brands talk about AI is now a strategic choice, not a technical one. Watch how this collides with the Capilano data-centre protest at your doorstep, where community resistance to AI infrastructure is already live on a BC campus. On the enrollment side, The Tyee's housing story quietly confirms the international-student contraction is now visibly reshaping BC campuses — a signal for every recruitment conversation this cycle. And in real estate, consolidation (CertifID/Closinglock) and the Compass-versus-MLS war show the plumbing of the industry is being fought over right now. Pay attention to language, governance, and who controls the pipes.
audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Thursday, October first, twenty twenty-six. The big theme today is who controls the AI story — the words, the governance, and the infrastructure — so let's start there.

The single most telling story this morning is out of Axios, and it's a marketing story disguised as a tech story. President Trump, flanked by the most powerful figures in Silicon Valley — Nvidia's Jensen Huang among them — has formally endorsed a new word for artificial intelligence: "superintelligence," or SI. This isn't a technical upgrade. It's a rebrand. And the reason they're doing it is right there in the reporting: leaders in Washington and in the Valley are genuinely worried that public backlash against AI and against data centres is going to slow the whole project down. So they're trying to shed what they're privately calling AI's toxic branding by giving it a shinier name.

Now, think about that from where you sit. When an entire trillion-dollar industry decides that its problem is the language, not the substance, that is a profound admission about the power of naming. And it's directly your lane. Every higher-ed client, every brokerage, every public institution you advise is going to face a version of this question: how do we talk about the AI we're deploying? The answer the industry is modelling right now — rebrand your way out of discomfort — is exactly the wrong lesson, and that's a contrarian post worth writing. Naming is strategy, yes, but renaming to dodge accountability is a tell. The brands that win trust will be the ones whose language matches what their systems actually do, and that ties straight back into your AI Search Readiness work — because generative search doesn't reward spin, it rewards substance it can verify.

The second AI story is quieter but it should stop you. STAT published a piece from a Stanford researcher describing how Claude analyzed a whole human genome in about thirty minutes for roughly five dollars. In two thousand nine, that same analysis took thirty people and nearly a year. His point isn't the speed — it's that we now have zero standards for interpreting what the AI produces. The capability has sprinted miles ahead of the guardrails. And that is the exact pattern you keep warning clients about through your public-institution governance lens. A FIPPA-bound university or a public agency can now adopt an AI tool that does something genuinely powerful long before anyone has written the policy for how to validate, store, or act on its output. That gap — capability outrunning governance — is the throughline of your entire thesis, and this genome story is a vivid, quotable example of it in a high-stakes domain. File it.

Now to the organizations worth watching closely, and interestingly the AI governance theme shows up right on a BC campus. The Capilano Courier, the student paper at Capilano University, is reporting on protests against AI data centre development. This matters because it's the superintelligence backlash I just described, playing out not in Washington but on the North Shore. Community resistance to AI infrastructure — the energy draw, the water use, the sense that this is being done to communities rather than with them — is the leading edge of the governance conversation. For anyone advising institutions on AI adoption, this is the warning flare: you cannot bolt on community trust after the fact. The audit question becomes, do you have a community-trust framework before you break ground, or before you sign the vendor contract? That's a strong POV piece.

Separately, North Shore News reports that Capilano University has secured two hundred and fifteen thousand dollars to advance Indigenous student success, landing the same week as its Truth and Reconciliation programming, including a fashion show on campus. Targeted funding tied to Indigenous student outcomes is a meaningful signal in the Canadian post-secondary landscape right now — it reflects where provincial and institutional priorities are flowing, and it's the kind of mission-aligned story that shapes brand and enrolment narratives.

On to higher education, where the story of the day is subtle but important. The Tyee reports that the drop in international students is actually easing the university housing crunch in British Columbia. Sit with that for a second. For years the narrative was that international enrolment was straining housing. Now the contraction is deep enough that you can see it in the vacancy numbers. That's not a feel-good story — it's a measurement of how far the decline has gone. For every recruitment and enrolment conversation you're in this cycle, this reframes the entire game. The job is no longer managing volume; it's protecting yield. When the top of the funnel shrinks, every single conversion matters more, which is precisely where AI-driven personalization and conversion optimization earn their keep. That's your higher-ed enrolment content angle: the shrinking funnel makes the case for AI in recruitment stronger, not weaker.

Reinforcing the same macro picture, The PIE News reports that Keystone Education Group — a major player in international student recruitment — posted a ten percent year-over-year drop in second-quarter revenue, blaming sustained recruitment pressure in the UK and US. When the recruitment infrastructure companies are reporting double-digit revenue declines, that's the industry telling you the contraction is structural, not a blip. The institutions that adapt their marketing operations fastest will take share from the ones still budgeting for yesterday's volumes.

Turning to marketing leadership, two CMO moves worth noting because they fit a pattern you should be tracking. Cava, the fast-casual chain, has hired John Ludeke — most recently chief brand officer at Dr. Squatch — as its new CMO, tasked with deepening consumer connection on top of an already strong growth run. And Molton Brown has named Laura Hogan CMO to lead a global brand push. The through-line: premium and high-growth brands are reaching for marketers who built emotional, distinctive brand platforms rather than pure performance operators. That's a signal about where the CMO mandate is heading — brand-building is back in the driver's seat, and it dovetails with the Gartner piece from yesterday about AI reshaping entry-level marketing needs. The senior brief is consolidating around brand and strategy while AI absorbs the executional layer.

In real estate, two stories about the plumbing of the industry being fought over right now. First, HousingWire reports CertifID is acquiring Closinglock, combining two wire-fraud-prevention platforms so threat intelligence can be shared across a much bigger brokerage customer base. Wire fraud remains one of the most damaging and underappreciated risks in a transaction, and consolidation here means the defensive tooling is getting more sophisticated and more centralized. For any brokerage operation, this is the security layer worth understanding.

Second, and more dramatic, RisMedia reports the escalating war between Compass and the MLS system. The California MLS, CRMLS, has rejected a Compass demand to loosen rules around public marketing of listings, and has gone further — launching an MLS legal defence fund and preparing a public response, accusing Compass of a scorched-earth campaign to consolidate market share. This is a genuinely important structural fight about who controls listing data and how homes get marketed. The mega-brokerage model versus the shared MLS commons — that tension will define brokerage operations and agent productivity for years, and it's a conversation worth being fluent in on the industry-advisory side.

Locally in Kamloops, a meaningful policy development: Castanet reports the province has opened the door to a Kamloops integrated court after years of advocacy. An integrated court model links the justice system with health and social services, and it's the kind of reform community advocates have pushed for a long time. It's a sign the province is responding to local pressure on the intersection of justice, addiction, and mental health.

On a heavier note, a Kamloops man has been charged after police in France flagged child sexual abuse material, triggering a local investigation. I'll leave it there, but it's in the local record this morning.

Nationally and globally, two items. Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected today to designate an oil pipeline to the West Coast as a project of national interest. That's a consequential energy and federalism decision with direct implications for British Columbia — watch how it lands provincially, especially against the backdrop of the ongoing BC election and the LNG Canada Phase Two news from earlier this week. And on a brighter note, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk launches to the International Space Station from Florida this morning — a genuine milestone for Canada's space program and a nice counterweight to a heavy news cycle.

Finally, one health item that clears the bar. STAT published an opinion piece from a transplant surgeon and researcher who studied GLP-1 weight-loss drugs in children, and his conclusion is that the results are reassuring. His argument is that intervening in childhood could spare kids decades of irreversible metabolic damage. This is a researcher reporting on his own data, so read it as an informed perspective rather than a definitive trial, but it's a meaningful data point in the fast-moving GLP-1 story — and it extends the "from patients to customers" thread we touched on earlier this week. The pediatric question is the next frontier, and the early read is cautiously positive.

So here's what I'd carry into the day, Midya. The AI industry just told us, out loud, that it thinks its biggest problem is a branding problem — and that's a gift to you, because it clarifies exactly where your voice is differentiated: substance and governance over spin. Watch the Capilano data-centre protest as a local, concrete version of that same tension, and let the shrinking international-student picture sharpen every enrolment pitch toward yield and conversion. The common thread across all of it is that capability is outrunning governance everywhere — in AI, in enrolment, in brokerage data. That's your terrain. Have a sharp Thursday, and if you write one thing today, make it the naming-is-strategy piece while it's hot.
